meta.title: Sports Tech VC Deal Sourcing Benchmark 2026
meta.subtitle: How 30 sports tech investors find, screen and close deals, and where the gaps are.

intro.heading: Why this benchmark, and why now
intro.subtitle: Capital has returned to sports tech. The competition to reach the right founders first has intensified with it.
body: Funding in the sector fell from $13.3B in 2021 to $2.3B in 2023, then recovered to $8.8B in 2025. Europe took the larger share of global investment for the first time, and 46 sports tech companies now carry valuations above a billion dollars.

The recovery has drawn more investors into sports tech than at any point in its history, competing for a limited number of credible companies through many of the same networks. How a fund finds companies now matters as much as how it judges them.

Sourcing is also the least documented part of the venture process. Firms describe their deal flow as proprietary, and there has been no shared reference point to measure that against. This study builds one, and it is designed to run every year.

Between April and July 2026, 30 investors with active sports tech portfolios answered the same questions on how they find companies, how many they review each month, which channels deliver and where the process slows down. They also gave us their fund profile: type, stage focus, geography, fund size and how many sports tech investments they have made, so the answers could be read in context. Each traced their last three investments back to source, which gave us 86 closed deals with an origin attached.

Thirty funds took part. Twenty agreed to be named as founding contributors, shown below, and ten took part confidentially. Every one of them receives a personalised snapshot comparing their own sourcing with the rest of the sample. The findings follow over the next three sections, with the method on the final page.

external_figures.note: Market figures are from GSTER 2026, not from this survey. Charts use study data only.

sections.heading: Where the deals come from
sections.subtitle: Six in ten investments started with an introduction from someone the investor already knew.
sections.intro: We asked every fund to trace its last three sports tech investments back to the moment the company first appeared on their radar. That produced 86 deals with a source attached to each one. Set against the roughly 1,700 companies these funds screen every month, the result is lopsided. One channel produces most of the deals, two of the seven produce almost none, and the channel that produces the second most is one of the lowest rated.

takeaways: Warm introductions are the biggest source of deals and the highest rated channel. Nothing else is close on either count.

Direct founder outreach is the second biggest source of deals and sits at the bottom of the quality ratings alongside data platforms, at 2.7 and 2.8 out of 5. Investors close one deal in seven through a route they rate poorly.
Events and research networks produced two deals each. Data platforms produced none at all, despite being used by 11 of the 30 funds.

sections.heading: Inside the sourcing process
sections.subtitle: Seven in ten investors are satisfied with their deal flow. Seven in ten of those same funds still name finding new companies as a top challenge.
sections.intro: 21 of the 30 funds rate their deal flow 4 or 5 out of 5. Fifteen of those same funds also name finding qualified companies they have not already seen as a top-two challenge. Investors are content with what reaches them and frustrated by what does not.

takeaways: 21 funds name finding qualified companies they have not already seen as a top-two challenge, and 15 name reaching companies before a formal process.
Time follows the same pattern. Identifying thesis-fit companies and initial screening are named by 16 funds each, ahead of pre-raise relationships at 11.

sections.heading: Going out to find deals
sections.subtitle: Nine in ten funds want to find companies themselves rather than wait for them. Most have nothing to do it with.
sections.intro: Outbound sourcing means a team spotting a company itself instead of waiting for it to arrive through an introduction or an email. Investors rate it among the best channels they have, and it produces 7% of their deals. Two in three funds run their sourcing without any data platform at all, and that includes half of the funds who say outbound matters most to them.

takeaways: Outbound is one of the three channels investors rate highly, and it produces 7% of their deals. Almost every fund says it wants more of it.
Of the 12 funds who want a lot more outbound sourcing, six have no data platform. None of the funds that do use one treats it as a primary source, and they rate its sports tech coverage 3.0 out of 5.
Asked what would help, investors chose introductions through a sector community (7.2 out of 10) and quarterly research on emerging subsectors (6.9). A data feed into their CRM came last at 5.7.

closing.heading: What this means for investors
closing.subtitle: Three readings of the 2026 benchmark, and an invitation to help build the 2027 one.
closing.intro: The study describes current practice across 30 funds. It shows what is common and what is rare, and it associates rather than proves. Read the following as prompts for your own process, not as prescriptions.

points.title: Relationships still carry the market
points.body: Warm introductions produced 59% of the 86 closed deals and are the highest rated channel at 4.3 out of 5. Co-investor and portfolio referrals close a further 14% at 4.2. No channel in the study has emerged as a substitute for either, which makes the quality of a fund's network its most consequential asset.

points.title: New names are the scarce input
points.body: 21 of the 30 funds name finding qualified companies they have not already seen as a top-two challenge, and 15 name reaching companies before a formal process. Satisfaction rises with screening volume, from 3.0 among the six funds reviewing fewer than ten companies a month to 4.5 among the eight reviewing more than 100.

points.title: Outbound is an intention more than a practice
points.body: 27 of the 30 funds want to increase proactive sourcing over the next year, and it currently accounts for 7% of closed deals. Two in three funds use no data platform, and the 11 that do rate its sports tech coverage 3.0 out of 5. The ambition is close to universal, the tooling is not.

cta.title: Take part in the 2027 edition
cta.body: The benchmark runs annually, and its value grows with the number of funds in it. Participating takes about ten minutes. Every fund receives a personalised snapshot comparing its own sourcing with the full sample, and can choose to be named or to take part confidentially.

methodology.heading: Method and data notes
methodology.subtitle: How the study was run, how the numbers were calculated, and where to read them carefully.
methodology.intro: The benchmark is built on 30 complete survey responses and 86 individually sourced investments. Everything below explains what sits behind the figures on the previous pages.

blocks.title: The sample
blocks.body: 30 venture investors with active sports tech portfolios, surveyed between April and July 2026. 67% are sector-focused funds, 70% invest at seed or early stage, and 87% manage $100M or less.

blocks.title: How figures are calculated
blocks.body: Percentages use all 30 funds unless stated. Challenge and time figures count funds placing an option in their first two choices. Closed deal shares draw on each fund's last three sports tech investments, 86 in total.

blocks.title: Screening estimate
blocks.body: The monthly screening figure applies the midpoint of each response band, with the open top band counted as 125 companies. It is an estimate of scale rather than a precise count.

blocks.title: Data notes
blocks.body: All figures are self-reported and grouped across the full sample. Comparisons between smaller groups rest on small numbers and should be read as indicative. Individual responses appear only in aggregate.

blocks.title: Quality ratings
blocks.body: Investors rated each channel they use from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high). Ratings exclude funds that do not use a given channel, so they reflect the experience of users only.

blocks.title: Disclosure
blocks.body: The study was designed and run by SportsTechX. Some of the forms of support tested in the survey resemble services SportsTechX offers.

note.title: Contributors and outside sources
note.body: 20 funds agreed to be named as founding contributors of this first edition, and 10 took part confidentially. The market figures cited on page 2 are drawn from the SportsTechX Global SportsTech Ecosystem Report 2026 rather than from this survey.
